How can we measure carbon dioxide? pH is the measure of acid in a solution.  When you add acid to water, its pH goes down. mainstream_body: Living Environment U2 CH 4 Extracting DNA from Strawberries Lab Question :  Can we use biochemistry lab techniques to extract DNA from strawberries?  What does purified DNA look like? Background Living things are made of the 4 classes of biomolecule :  Nucleic acids, proteins, carbohydrates and lipids. DNA is a nucleic acid and there is DNA in every cell. DNA is the “code of life” because it stores critical information, hereditary information that is copied during the cell cycle and passed to offspring, and coding information in the form of genes.  Genes are transcribed into RNA, RNA is usually translated into proteins and proteins carry out vital functions in cells. Each class of biomolecule has unique chemical properties, that is, each class behaves in a unique way in different solutions.  We can use these differences in behavior to purify a class of biomolecule from a mixture.  We can use DNA’s unique chemical properties to separate it from all the other types of molecule that make a strawberry. The technique we will use can be used with any living tissue, but strawberries are fun to work with:  They smell good, they are a bright color and they have lots of DNA, 4 times more than other types of cells!  If you like this experiment, you can easily repeat it at home with a piece of an onion, apple or banana. Scientists study human DNA by purifying it from blood, saliva, inner cheek cells and other sources. In addition to helping us learn about how life works, purified DNA can help scientists diagnose diseases, fight cancer, solve crimes and learn about a person’s genetic heritage. Pre-lab Questions: What are the 4 classes of biomolecule? To which class of biomolecule does DNA belong? Which type of monomer is linked together to form DNA polymers? Which other important information molecule is made from the same monomers as DNA? What are the 2 main functions of DNA? Predict what purified DNA will look like. Materials for each pair of students 2 strawberries 20 mls DNA Extraction Buffer Ziplock baggie Coffee filter 1 clear, plastic cup 91% isopropyl alcohol Toothpicks Storage container Procedure Place strawberries in baggie. Add 20 mls DNA Extraction Buffer Close the baggy tightly. Gently crush the strawberries, flattening them, breaking them up, but avoiding lots of bubbles. Place the coffee filter over the plastic cup Pour the crushed strawberry mixture onto the filter. Let the liquid drain through the filter, keeping chunks of strawberry in the filter. Remove the filter and set aside. Pour 91% isopropyl alcohol down the side of the cup, onto the surface of the pink liquid.  Gently swirl, or gently stir with the toothpick. Watch the DNA appear in a layer between the alcohol and the strawberry liquid. If you would like to take your DNA home, wrap the strands of DNA around the toothpick to pick it up and move it to a storage container. Analysis Questions When could you first see the strawberry DNA? Describe the appearance of the DNA. For each step of the purification listed below, decide whether you use physical method or a chemical method to extract DNA? mainstream_body: Living Environment U2 CH 4 Extracting DNA from Strawberries Lab Question :  Can we use biochemistry lab techniques to extract DNA from strawberries?  What does purified DNA look like? Background Living things are made of the 4 classes of biomolecule :  Nucleic acids, proteins, carbohydrates and lipids. DNA is a nucleic acid and there is DNA in every cell. DNA is the “code of life” because it stores critical information, hereditary information that is copied during the cell cycle and passed to offspring, and coding information in the form of genes.  Genes are transcribed into RNA, RNA is usually translated into proteins and proteins carry out vital functions in cells. Each class of biomolecule has unique chemical properties, that is, each class behaves in a unique way in different solutions.  We can use these differences in behavior to purify a class of biomolecule from a mixture.  We can use DNA’s unique chemical properties to separate it from all the other types of molecule that make a strawberry. The technique we will use can be used with any living tissue, but strawberries are fun to work with:  They smell good, they are a bright color and they have lots of DNA, 4 times more than other types of cells!  If you like this experiment, you can easily repeat it at home with a piece of an onion, apple or banana. Scientists study human DNA by purifying it from blood, saliva, inner cheek cells and other sources. In addition to helping us learn about how life works, purified DNA can help scientists diagnose diseases, fight cancer, solve crimes and learn about a person’s genetic heritage. Pre-lab Questions: What are the 4 classes of biomolecule? To which class of biomolecule does DNA belong? Which type of monomer is linked together to form DNA polymers? Which other important information molecule is made from the same monomers as DNA? What are the 2 main functions of DNA? Predict what purified DNA will look like. Materials for each pair of students 2 strawberries 20 mls DNA Extraction Buffer Ziplock baggie Coffee filter 1 clear, plastic cup 91% isopropyl alcohol Toothpicks Storage container Procedure Place strawberries in baggie. Add 20 mls DNA Extraction Buffer Close the baggy tightly. Gently crush the strawberries, flattening them, breaking them up, but avoiding lots of bubbles. Place the coffee filter over the plastic cup Pour the crushed strawberry mixture onto the filter. Let the liquid drain through the filter, keeping chunks of strawberry in the filter. Remove the filter and set aside. Pour 91% isopropyl alcohol down the side of the cup, onto the surface of the pink liquid.  Gently swirl, or gently stir with the toothpick. Watch the DNA appear in a layer between the alcohol and the strawberry liquid. If you would like to take your DNA home, wrap the strands of DNA around the toothpick to pick it up and move it to a storage container. Analysis Questions When could you first see the strawberry DNA? mainstream_body: Living Environment U2 CH 4 Extracting DNA from Strawberries Lab Question :  Can we use biochemistry lab techniques to extract DNA from strawberries?  What does purified DNA look like? Background Living things are made of the 4 classes of biomolecule :  Nucleic acids, proteins, carbohydrates and lipids. DNA is a nucleic acid and there is DNA in every cell. DNA is the “code of life” because it stores critical information, hereditary information that is copied during the cell cycle and passed to offspring, and coding information in the form of genes.  Genes are transcribed into RNA, RNA is usually translated into proteins and proteins carry out vital functions in cells. Each class of biomolecule has unique chemical properties, that is, each class behaves in a unique way in different solutions.  We can use these differences in behavior to purify a class of biomolecule from a mixture.  We can use DNA’s unique chemical properties to separate it from all the other types of molecule that make a strawberry. The technique we will use can be used with any living tissue, but strawberries are fun to work with:  They smell good, they are a bright color and they have lots of DNA, 4 times more than other types of cells!  If you like this experiment, you can easily repeat it at home with a piece of an onion, apple or banana. Scientists study human DNA by purifying it from blood, saliva, inner cheek cells and other sources. In addition to helping us learn about how life works, purified DNA can help scientists diagnose diseases, fight cancer, solve crimes and learn about a person’s genetic heritage. Pre-lab Questions: What are the 4 classes of biomolecule? To which class of biomolecule does DNA belong? Which type of monomer is linked together to form DNA polymers? Which other important information molecule is made from the same monomers as DNA? What are the 2 main functions of DNA? Predict what purified DNA will look like. Materials for each pair of students 2 strawberries 20 mls DNA Extraction Buffer Ziplock baggie Coffee filter 1 clear, plastic cup 91% isopropyl alcohol Toothpicks Storage container Procedure Place strawberries in baggie. Add 20 mls DNA Extraction Buffer Close the baggy tightly. Gently crush the strawberries, flattening them, breaking them up, but avoiding lots of bubbles. Place the coffee filter over the plastic cup Pour the crushed strawberry mixture onto the filter. Let the liquid drain through the filter, keeping chunks of strawberry in the filter. Remove the filter and set aside. Pour 91% isopropyl alcohol down the side of the cup, onto the surface of the pink liquid.  Gently swirl, or gently stir with the toothpick. Watch the DNA appear in a layer between the alcohol and the strawberry liquid. If you would like to take your DNA home, wrap the strands of DNA around the toothpick to pick it up and move it to a storage container. Analysis Questions When could you first see the strawberry DNA? Describe the appearance of the DNA. For each step of the purification listed below, decide whether you use physical method or a chemical method to extract DNA? Smashing the strawberries Adding detergent and salt to the strawberry mixture Adding alcohol to the strawberry mixture Using a toothpick to pull the DNA out of the cup When you pulled the DNA out of the cup, which classes of biomolecule were left behind in the mixture? Think about the food you ate at your most recent mea l.  Was there DNA in your food? How do you know? What are some things that scientists can learn by studying purified DNA? mainstream_body: Living Environment U2 CH 4 Extracting DNA from Strawberries Lab Question :  Can we use biochemistry lab techniques to extract DNA from strawberries?  What does purified DNA look like? Background Living things are made of the 4 classes of biomolecule :  Nucleic acids, proteins, carbohydrates and lipids. DNA is a nucleic acid and there is DNA in every cell. DNA is the “code of life” because it stores critical information, hereditary information that is copied during the cell cycle and passed to offspring, and coding information in the form of genes.  Genes are transcribed into RNA, RNA is usually translated into proteins and proteins carry out vital functions in cells. Each class of biomolecule has unique chemical properties, that is, each class behaves in a unique way in different solutions.  We can use these differences in behavior to purify a class of biomolecule from a mixture.  We can use DNA’s unique chemical properties to separate it from all the other types of molecule that make a strawberry. The technique we will use can be used with any living tissue, but strawberries are fun to work with:  They smell good, they are a bright color and they have lots of DNA, 4 times more than other types of cells!  If you like this experiment, you can easily repeat it at home with a piece of an onion, apple or banana. Scientists study human DNA by purifying it from blood, saliva, inner cheek cells and other sources. In addition to helping us learn about how life works, purified DNA can help scientists diagnose diseases, fight cancer, solve crimes and learn about a person’s genetic heritage. Pre-lab Questions: What are the 4 classes of biomolecule? To which class of biomolecule does DNA belong? Which type of monomer is linked together to form DNA polymers? Which other important information molecule is made from the same monomers as DNA? What are the 2 main functions of DNA? Predict what purified DNA will look like. Materials for each pair of students 2 strawberries 20 mls DNA Extraction Buffer Ziplock baggie Coffee filter 1 clear, plastic cup 91% isopropyl alcohol Toothpicks Storage container Procedure Place strawberries in baggie. Add 20 mls DNA Extraction Buffer Close the baggy tightly. Gently crush the strawberries, flattening them, breaking them up, but avoiding lots of bubbles. Place the coffee filter over the plastic cup Pour the crushed strawberry mixture onto the filter. Let the liquid drain through the filter, keeping chunks of strawberry in the filter. Remove the filter and set aside. Pour 91% isopropyl alcohol down the side of the cup, onto the surface of the pink liquid.  Gently swirl, or gently stir with the toothpick. Watch the DNA appear in a layer between the alcohol and the strawberry liquid. If you would like to take your DNA home, wrap the strands of DNA around the toothpick to pick it up and move it to a storage container. Analysis Questions When could you first see the strawberry DNA? Describe the appearance of the DNA. For each step of the purification listed below, decide whether you use physical method or a chemical method to extract DNA? Think about the food you ate at your most recent mea l.  Was there DNA in your food? How do you know? What are some things that scientists can learn by studying purified DNA? mainstream_body: Graham Cracker Plate Tectonics Lab Name______________________ Just a little info… The Theory of Plate Tectonics states that the crust of the Earth is composed of seven major plates and numerous smaller plates. These plates “ride” on the hot plastic upper mantle called the asthenosphere. This theory also says that most of these plates are in motion, creating a variety of interactions at the plate boundaries. As plate boundaries, plates may converge, diverge, or slip (lateral) past each other in a horizontal motion. In addition, some plates may appear to be inactive. Pre-lab Questions: What is subduction? Explain what a divergent boundary is. Explain what a convergent boundary is. Explain what a transform boundary is. True or False. When sea-floor spreading occurs, new crust is added to the ocean floor. Explain what convection currents are. Materials (per group) Graham crackers (2 whole crackers) Spoonful of cool whip or frosting (per group) Knives or spoons Wax paper or paper plates Cup of water Procedure- Sea Floor Spreading Each whole graham cracker into four pieces by following the perforations on the cracker. Each section of the lab will use 2 pieces Using the knives or spoons, spread a thick layer of cool whip in the center of the paper plate or wax paper. Lay two pieces of the graham cracker side by side on top of the cool whip. To imitate sea-floor spreading, press down lightly on the crackers as you slowly push down and apart in opposite directions. Do not push the crackers more than 1 centimeter apart! Remove the graham crackers from the cool whip. Questions What happened to the cool whip between the crackers? What do the graham crackers represent? What does the cool whip represent? Procedure Convergent Plate Boundarie s, Subduction Zone Now lay two graham cracker and end-to-end (against each other) on top of the cool whip. Push the two “plate” models slowly toward each other and observe which plate rides up over the other. On the actual surface of the earth, the lower and more dense plate is subducted. Questions Which plate is more dense: continental or oceanic? Which plate will subduct or sink under the other? How do the colliding graham crackers model a subduction zone? Procedure Convergent Boundaries Continental Crust Use two new pieces of graham cracker. Dip one end of each of the two graham crackers two centimeters into a cup of water. IMMEDIATELY remove the crackers and lay them end to end on the cool whip with the wet edges nearly touching. Slowly push the two crackers together , as in the previous section. Questions What happens to the wet ends of the graham crackers? In what way do the wet crackers act more like the real crustal plates than the dry crackers? When two continental plates collide in a convergent boundary, they squeeze together to form what? Procedure Transform Boundaries Use the two remaining graham cracker pieces for this part of the lab. Fit the two pieces together side side on top of the cool whip on the paper. Place one hand on each of the cracker pieces and push them together by applying steady, moderate pressure. At the same time, also push one of the pieces away from you while pulling the other toward you. If you do this correctly, the cracker should hold while you increase the push-pull pressure, but will finally break from the opposite forces. Questions Why is this movement often described as “horizontal” sliding? What natural disaster occurs often near this type of boundary? Hurricanes Home work Name ___________________________ Hurricanes Engines of Destruction Photograph courtesy NASA/GSFC Hurricanes are giant, spiraling tropical storms that can pack wind speeds of over 160 miles (257 kilometers) an hour and unleash more than 2.4 trillion gallons (9 trillion liters) of rain a day. These same tropical storms are known as cyclones in the northern Indian Ocean and Bay of Bengal, and as typhoons in the western Pacific Ocean. The Atlantic Ocean’s hurricane season peaks from mid-August to late October and averages five to six hurricanes per year. Hurricanes begin as tropical disturbances in warm ocean waters with surface temperatures of at least 80 degrees Fahrenheit (26.5 degrees Celsius). These low pressure systems are fed by energy from the warm seas. If a storm achieves wind speeds of 38 miles (61 kilometers) an hour, it becomes known as a tropical depression. A tropical depression becomes a tropical storm, and is given a name, when its sustained wind speeds top 39 miles (63 kilometers) an hour. When a storm’s sustained wind speeds reach 74 miles (119 kilometers) an hour it becomes a hurricane and earns a category rating of 1 to 5 on the Saffir-Simpson scale. Hurricanes are enormous heat engines that generate energy on a staggering scale. They draw heat from warm, moist ocean air and release it through condensation of water vapor in thunderstorms. Hurricanes spin around a low-pressure center known as the “eye.” Sinking air makes this 20- to 30-mile-wide (32- to 48-kilometer-wide) area notoriously calm. But the eye is surrounded by a circular “eye wall” that hosts the storm’s strongest winds and rain. These storms bring destruction ashore in many different ways. When a hurricane makes landfall it often produces a devastating storm surge that can reach 20 feet (6 meters) high and extend nearly 100 miles (161 kilometers). Ninety percent of all hurricane deaths result from storm surges. A hurricane’s high winds are also destructive and may spawn tornadoes. Torrential rains cause further damage by spawning floods and landslides, which may occur many miles inland. The best defense against a hurricane is an accurate forecast that gives people time to get out of its way. The National Hurricane Center issues hurricane watches for storms that may endanger communities, and hurricane warnings for storms that will make landfall within 24 hours. mainstream_body: Progressive Mathematics Initiative www.njctl.org Mathematics Curriculum Chapter Plan Title: Equations & Inequalities Grade Level: Grade Length of Time: weeks Chapter Summary: This chapter will introduce students to different properties equations can have. They will be able to combine like terms, solve multi-step equations, and deal with inequalities. Also, they will identify what the associative, commutative, and distributive properties are. Learning Targets PARCC Major Clusters; Supporting Clusters; Additional Clusters Domain: Expressions and Equations Cluster: Use properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions Standard #: Standard: 7.EE.1 Apply properties of operations as strategies to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients. 7.EE.2 Understand that rewriting an expression in different forms in a problem context can shed light on the problem and how the quantities in it are related. For example, a + 0.05a = 1.05a means that ""increase by 5%"" is the same as ""multiply by 1.05."" Cluster: Solve real-life and mathematical problems using numerical and algebraic expressions and equations. Standard #s: Standards: 7.EE.3 Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies. For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation. 7.EE.4 Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities. Solve word problems leading to equations of the form + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach. For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width? Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form + q > r or + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem. For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions Domain Standards for Math Practice Standard#: Standard: MP1 Making sense of problems and persevere in solving them. MP2 Reason abstractly and quantitatively. MP3 Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others. MP4 Model with mathematics. MP5 Use appropriate tools strategically. MP6 Attend to precision. MP7 Look for and make use of structure. MP8 Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning. Chapter Essential Question How are equations solved? What are different properties of equations and how can they help solve them? What happens when two sides of an equation are not equal? Chapter Enduring Understandings: Equations can be solved using different properties. Sometimes there is more than one step to solve in an equation. Inequalities are used when solving for real life application problems. Chapter Objectives: Students will examine commutative and associative properties of different equations. Students will combine like terms within an equation and learn to use the distributive property to solve equations. Students will solve multi-step equations involving different techniques. Students will graph and solve inequalities involving addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. mainstream_body: Progressive Mathematics Initiative www.njctl.org Mathematics Curriculum Chapter Plan Title: Equations & Inequalities Grade Level: Grade Length of Time: weeks Chapter Summary: This chapter will introduce students to different properties equations can have. They will be able to combine like terms, solve multi-step equations, and deal with inequalities. Also, they will identify what the associative, commutative, and distributive properties are. Learning Targets PARCC Major Clusters; Supporting Clusters; Additional Clusters Domain: Expressions and Equations Cluster: Use properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions Standard #: Standard: 7.EE.1 Apply properties of operations as strategies to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients. 7.EE.2 Understand that rewriting an expression in different forms in a problem context can shed light on the problem and how the quantities in it are related. For example, a + 0.05a = 1.05a means that ""increase by 5%"" is the same as ""multiply by 1.05."" Cluster: Solve real-life and mathematical problems using numerical and algebraic expressions and equations. Standard #s: Standards: 7.EE.3 Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies. For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation. 7.EE.4 Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities. Solve word problems leading to equations of the form + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach. For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width? Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form + q > r or + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem. For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions Domain Standards for Math Practice Standard#: Standard: MP1 Making sense of problems and persevere in solving them. MP2 Reason abstractly and quantitatively. MP3 Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others. MP4 Model with mathematics. MP5 Use appropriate tools strategically. MP6 Attend to precision. MP7 Look for and make use of structure. MP8 Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning. Chapter Essential Question How are equations solved? What are different properties of equations and how can they help solve them? What happens when two sides of an equation are not equal? Chapter Enduring Understandings: Equations can be solved using different properties. Sometimes there is more than one step to solve in an equation. Inequalities are used when solving for real life application problems. Chapter Objectives: Students will examine commutative and associative properties of different equations. Students will combine like terms within an equation and learn to use the distributive property to solve equations. Students will solve multi-step equations involving different techniques. Students will graph and solve inequalities involving addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. (MS-PS3-4) Energy is spontaneously transferred out of hotter regions or objects and into colder ones. After modeling addition and subtraction with both the Interactive White Board and manipulatives, students will be able to fluently add and subtract within 5. Various activities and games will also be used to deepen students’ understandings. Learning Targets Domain Operations & Algebraic Thinking Cluster Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from. Standard Standard K.OA.1 Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. K.OA.2 Solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10, e.g., by using objects or drawings to represent the problem. K.OA.3 Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 5 = 2 + 3 and 5 = 4 + 1). K.OA.4 For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record the answer with a drawing or equation. K.OA.5 Fluently add and subtract within 5. Unit Essential Question: How Why do I need to add and subtract? What strategies can I use to add and subtract? Unit Enduring Understanding Quantities can be combined or taken apart. Unit Objectives Students will be able to show that addition is the putting together and subtraction is the taking apart of things. Students will be able to identify the addition, subtraction and equal signs. Students will be able to understand addition through addition patterns, counting on, and addition loops. Students will represent addition and subtract both horizontally and vertically. Students will be able to find a missing addend. Students will model subtraction with both pictures / objects and connecting cubes. Students will be able to tell is a situation is representing addition or subtraction. Evidence of Learning Formative Assessments: SMART Response questions used throughout the unit. Parental Care Name: _____________________ Grade PSI Elephants are a type of animal that shows a lot of parental care. An elephant calf is born after spending two years developing inside the mother. The entire elephant herd will welcome the new calf by touching it with their trunks. Elephants do not build nests or dens. They sleep on the ground in forests or grasses. The baby elephant is sheltered in this way too. An elephant calf has poor eyesight and depends on the mother for survival. It feeds on milk from the mother until it is about three years old. After it is able to walk steadily, it also finds its own vegetation and water. Elephant calves are protected by the entire herd. When danger approaches, the herd will surround the calves. Calves learn elephant behaviors by watching adults and playing with one another. Animals that show parental care usually provide the offspring with food, shelter, protection and education. Describe three ways that elephants provide parental care to their offspring. ________________________________________ _________________________________________ ________________________________________ _________________________________________ ________________________________________ _________________________________________ Baby Robins Activity Name___________________________ Grade PSI Teacher’s Notes Reinforce the idea that both parents and offspring have behaviors that help the offspring to survive. For robins, parent’s behaviors include sitting on the nest to keep it warm, feeding the chicks, and protecting the chicks by chasing away predators. Behaviors displayed by the chicks include chirping when hungry or threatened and opening their mouths when food comes. Procedure: Two students will be designated “parent robins”. They will be in charge of chasing away predators (make sure the students understand a predator is bad!), sitting with the chicks (this simulates sitting on the nest for warmth and comfort), and feeding the chicks (you can use any candy, cookie , etc. to simulate worms/insects Another student will be designated “predator”. They can be another bird (ex., crow) , or a dog, cat, etc. When called on, they will circle the nest until confronted by a parent robin. Section off an area in the classroom/outdoors and say that this area is the “nest”. All chicks must stay in the nest because they cannot fly yet and are too young to go off on their own. Have both of the parents stay with the nest and remark on how everything is going well. Ask the “chicks” if they are hungry. If so, what can they do to signal the p arents to get food? ( CHIRP ).  Have a parent go off when they hear this and get the “treats”. When they come back, what behavior (make sure you use the word “behavior”) can the chicks do to make sure they are fed? ( Have them hold their hands out to represent an actual chick opening their mouths. Once they receive something to eat, have them close their hands). Next, simulate an unwanted intruder/predator around the nest. Send both the parents off to get food, leaving the chicks alone. Have your predator start to come up to the nest. Once again, have the students guess what behavior they should do ( Chicks should cheap loudly to get their parent’s attention, while the parent robins fly back and start chasing away the intruder ). Have the intruder run around the nest a bit before finally submitting to the parents and running away. Finally, end with “nighttime”. Ask where the mom bird would be ( in the ne st while the dad bird would be somewhere in the area keeping watch ). Ask how the chicks would be feeling ( omforted, full, happy, safe , etc. ).If time allows, discuss other patterns in behavior that can be observed among other animals. Examples: Kittens mewing, puppies barking, babies crying, ducklings lining up and following mom, baby buffalo standing up quickly after birth to follow the herd, etc. Baby Robins Activity Name___________________________ Grade PSI Introduction: The American robin is a bird that we all see in our backyards, especially in the spring and summer. They have dark feathers with bright orange bellies. We usually see robins in the spring when they begin to build their nests. Robin m oms will lay 3 -5 eggs and keep watch over them as they hatch. When the chicks hatch, they need a lot of help from mom and dad to row big and strong . Luckily, r obins are excellent parents! When the chicks are born, mom and dad robin take turns feeding them worms, berries, and insects. They also “dive” at other birds or animals that get too close to the nest. They don’t want these animals disturbing their chicks. At nighttime, as the chicks get older, mom robin still sits in the nest with them, comforting them and keeping them warm and protected. aby animals know how to call for mom and dad. E ven baby humans know how to call for help!  Have you ever heard a baby in your family cry? Usually, they want to be fed, changed or just hugged. Wild babies do the same thing! Robin chicks will “chirp” when they are hungry or scared. They are saying, “Mom! Dad! Come to me!” When their parents come back with food, chicks will poke their faces out of the nest and open their mouths wide showing them where to put the food! These are behaviors that help them survive In this activity, members of the class are going to pretend they are robin chicks. Two students will be the parent robins and tend to the young, just like real robin parents would do. Be sure to chase away any intruders! mainstream_body: PMI – 2 Grade Geometry Unit Lab – 2 Dimensional Shapes Overview: Students will build two dimensional shapes out of straws and twist ties. Then, they will play game in which the teacher or student will describe a 2 dimensional shape they have drawn while the other partner or group members produce that shape. Materials per student: 10 - 12 pipe cleaners cut in half 6 plastic straws cut in half (short straws) 6 plastic straws left whole (long straws) Note: plastic bar straws are thinner and easier to connect but they are harder to find. Some grocery stores carry them but you may also find them at party or restaurant supply stores. Lab Day 1: Teacher instructs students on how to make an angle by connecting two long straws and a twist tie or pipe cleaner. It helps to first fold the twist tie or pipe cleaner in half so that is stays firmly in the straw ends. Have the students make different types of angles: right, obtuse, acute. This is just an introduction to the vocabulary but they are not required to learn it yet. Next, show how to make a 2 dimensional shape by connecting angles. Let the students explore making different shapes and describing them. Next, play a short game where the teacher describes the shape she or he has drawn previously. The students then have to build it according to the directions and guess what it is called. Examples: Build a shape that has two short, parallel sides opposite each other and two long parallel sides opposite each other. Make sure you have right angles. What is this shape called? (rectangle) Build a shape where none of the 3 sides are parallel. What shape is it? (triangle) Build a shape that has four sides. Two of opposite sides are the same length, and the other set of opposite sides are not the same length. One pair of sides are not parallel. What shape is it? (trapezoid) Create a shape that has 4 angles where only the opposite angles are the same. (rhombus, parallelogram, or quadrilateral) Lab Day 2 (partners or small group): Using a partition such as a privacy folder, students take turns drawing a shape and describing it to their partner or group to build. PMI – 2 Grade Geometry Unit Lab – Dimensional Shapes Lab Day 1 Overview: Students will build a three dimensional cube out of straws and pipe cleaners. They will then dip them in a soap solution to no tice the films that are created in the cube frames. Building the cubes will reinforce their understanding of faces and vertices. mainstream_body: Chemical Weathering Lab 4th grade PSI Teacher’s Notes: Having students conduct Mohs Hardness Test requires a lot of preparation. Rock samples and the materials used to test them need to be collected and ready. Divide students for this activity however you think will work best and depending on the number of supplies you have. Make sure you are very familiar with the procedure of the Mohs Hardness Test before you lead this lab, so you will be able to circulate and help students as they work. Chemical Weathering Lab Name: _____________________ _____ 4th grade PSI Lab Question How does chemical weathering affect different types of rocks? Before You Begin How might carbonated water be like acid rain? ___________________________ _____________________ ___________________________ _____________________ ___________________________ _____________________ Purpose uring this experiment, you will create a model of chemical weathering. This experiment will span two class periods but at least four days; the first day you will create your model and take some measurements, and the second day of the experiment you will take more measurements after you have waited for the chemical weathering to occur. While you are conducting the lab, make sure to fill out the charts for Mohs Hardness Test as you work. There are separate charts for Day 1 and Day 2. Conclusion Questions should be answered after the lab is complete Materials: package of plastic 8 oz drinking glasses or cups 1 liter bottle of club soda or seltzer water masking tape clock or watch 3 fragments of each of the following rock samples: limestone, marble, granite, and sandstone 1 copper penny 1 steel nail 1 piece of quartz Procedure : Day 1 Fill four cups or glasses three-fourths full of carbonated water (club soda or seltzer water) Fill four cups or glasses three fourths full of tap water. Place masking ta pe on the cups and label them: mestone and carbonated water limeston e and tap water marble and carbonated water marble and tap water granite and carbonated water granite and tap water ndstone and carbonated water sandstone and tap water Place the appropriate rock sample fragments into each labeled cup. Set aside a fragment of each type of rock for a control. These jars will sit for 3 or more days. Perform the Moh Hardness Test (instructions below) on the control samples that you set aside and record your results on the chart below Procedure: Day 2 (3 or more days later…) Remove the rocks from the jars and perform the Mohs Hardness Test on each, including your control fragments. Record your results on the chart below. Mohs Hardness Test Procedure ut each mineral sample on top of its name on the chart. Starting with the first mineral, test how hard it is by trying to scratch it. First try to scratch it with your fingernail, then the copper, then the nail, then the quartz. Be careful! Sometimes something that’s much softer than something else will leave a line of powder that looks a lot like a scratch. If you think you have a scratch, rub at it with your thumb. If it’s just powder, it’ll rub off, but if it’s really a scratch, it’ll still be there. If you can scratch the mineral with your fingernail, put an “X” in the “Fingernail” column. If not, leave it blank and go on to the next column. If you can scratch the mineral with copper, put an “X” in that column. Keep going until you have tried to scratch the sample with all of your hardness testers. If nothing makes a scratch, leave all of the columns blank. Your testing materials will leave a scratch if they are the same hardness as or harder than the sample. If you get a scratch, the hardness of the mineral is probably somewhere between the hardness of that testing material and the one before it. So, for example, if the quartz and the nail leave scratches on a sample but the penny doesn’t, the hardness of the sample is most likely somewhere between copper, hardness 3, and steel, hardness 5.5. So split the dif ference and call it a 4 on Mohs Hardness Scale. Write this number down in the “Hardness” column. If not even the quartz will make a scratch, your sample is harder than quartz (7), so write “>7” in the “Hardness” column. If all of the tests produce a scratch, your sample is softer than fingernails (2.5), so write “<2.5” in the “Hardness” column. Repeat this procedure for all of your samples. When you’re done, list the rock samples in order of hardness, from softest (lowest number) to hardest (highest number). You now have a relative hardness scale of your samples. mainstream_body: Design an Energy Device Lab 4th grade PSI Teacher’s Notes: In this lab, students will use what they have learned in the past two activities to work at creating their own device that converts energy. This will probably be a challenge to many students, but make sure to remind them to keep thinking back to the activities they have already done for ideas. Consider having students work in pairs or small groups on this lab, or have the option to work either individually or in a group. The most important part of this lab is to get students really thinking about how they could design a device that convert s energy. They will also have the opportunity to try to build their device, but it is less important that the device they build actually works or that they are able to build it exactly like they designed it. In their attempts to build, students must be able to define any constraints they run into (materials, cost, time), but they do not need to fix them. The materials list for this lab is flexible. It is a good idea to have some small motors and other materials that students used in the past two activities, since they are familiar with these. Materials (per class) Clicker Task box (filled with tasks on separate slips of paper) Candy Procedure Read through this procedure once. Then watch as your teacher demonstrates it. When it is your turn, follow her example. One student will be assigned the role of “trainer”. One student will be assigned the role of “ animal The trainer will pick a task out of the task box. This is the behavior that you want your animal to do. Animal : Your job is to try to do a specific task. The only feedback you will receive is a click from the trainer. Every time you do something that is similar to your task, the trainer will use the clicker. Since there is no way for you to know what your task is, begin by trying random things (walk around in different directions, pat your head etc.). When you receive a click, think about what you just did. Try it again or try a variation of it. Keep trying new things until you receive more clicks. Eventually, you will discover your task and receive your reward! Trainer: Your job is to train you r animal how to do their task. They do not know what they are supposed to be doing. The only feedback you are allowed to give is a click. Since your animal knows that a click is a good thing, this positive reinforcement will help them to know that they are on the right track. When they do something close to their task, click them once. If they move away from or do something different from their task, do nothing. Only give a click if they do something similar to their task. As they get closer to their task, give additional clicks. When they finally figure out their task, reward them with a click and a piece of candy. Analysis In any animal training that uses a clicker, the first important step is to train the animal to have a positive response to the clicker. How does this happen? mainstream_body: Build ing a Food Web Activity Name: _________________________ Grade PSI Experimental Question How is energy transferred between organisms? What is the relationship between all living things in an ecosystem? Purpose In this activity you will explore how energy is transferred between organisms.  Using the organisms commonly found in a forest you will create a food web to show the relationships between all living organisms.  Once the food web is create you will identify different groups of organisms that play a role in each ecosystem. Materials Poster paper Tape or glue Scissors Markers String or yarn Organisms in the Food Web Grass Pine Trees Salamander Elk Skunk Squirrel Raccoon Mountain Lion Finch Butterfly Fruit Coyotes Procedure Orient a piece of poster paper in portrait layout (narrow side on the top). Label the paper “Forest Food Web” Cut out the organism labels and begin to arrange them on your paper to create a food web. Once you have the organisms arranged, check your results with a partner or you teacher. Using tape or glue attach the organisms in their correct position within the food web. Cut out or draw pictures of each organism in the ecosystem. With either the string or markers connect each organisms that interacts with another. Label the three different groups of organisms in the food web; producers, primary consumers and secondary consumers. Analysis Questions What organisms are the producers in your food web? ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Describe the difference between a primary and secondary consumer. ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ In the food web, were there any omnivores? If so what organisms? ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Why are food webs helpful? What information do they provide? ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ _________________________________________________________________________________________________ _______________________________ Describe what is the original source of food/energy in a food web? ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Unit Lesson Plan – Ecosystem Dynamics Teacher: Time Frame: days Grade: 5th Grade School: Subject: PSI Middle School Science NGSS /DCI 5-LS2.A: Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems The food of almost any kind of animal can be traced back to plants.  Organisms are related in food webs in which some animals eat plants for food and other animals eat the animals that eat plants.  Some organisms, such as fungi and bacteria, break down dead organisms (both plants or plants parts and animals) and therefore operate as “decomposers.”  Decomposition eventually restores (recycles) some materials back to the soil.  Organisms can survive only in environments in which their particular needs are met.  A healthy ecosystem is one in which multiple species of different types are each able to meet their needs in a relatively stable web of life.  Newly introduced species can damage the balance of an ecosystem. (5-LS2-1) http://www.nextgenscience.org/5ls2-ecosystems-interactions-energy-dynamics 5-LS2.B: Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems Matter cycles between the air and soil and among plants, animals, and microbes as these organisms live and die.  Organisms obtain gases, and water, from the environment, and release waste matter (gas, liquid, or solid) back into the environment. (5-LS2-1) Instructional Objective: 5-LS2-1 Develop a model to describe the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers, and the environment. ssential Questions (What questions will the student be able to answer as a result of the instruction?) How can a food web be used to help observe interactions between organisms in an environment? What are the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers and the Sun in an ecosystem? How is matter transferred through an ecosystem? How can an organism maintain its population in an ecosystem?  What factors can threaten a species? By the end of this unit, students will know: All food webs rely on the s un for its energy source and producers to create their own food. Energy and mass are transferred from one organism to the next as it is eaten. Decomposers take dead material and recycle it back into usable material. Ecosystems are very fragile and require a perfect balance of predator and prey. By the end of this unit, students will be able to: Create a food web Explain the importance of producers, consumers and decomposers in an ecosystem Observe and analyze factors that aid decomposition Describe the flow of energy and mass through a food web Make conclusions about an ecosystem’s chances for survival based on factors such as overpopulation or overhunting. mainstream_body: Changing States of Matter Lab Name: ______________________________ Grade PSI Science Score: ______________ / 5 Experiment Question: What happens to the mass of a substance when it changes phases between solid and liquid Hypothesis Starters: How are a solid and a liquid similar How are they different? Explain your thinking. Draw a picture at a molecular level to show how mol ecules are arranged in a solid. 3. Draw a picture at a molecular level to show how molecules are arranged in a liquid. Purpose These experiments will help you observe what happens to the mass of a substance when it changes phases from solid to l iquid or from liquid to solid. Solids often have molecules that are locked in a specific place. Liquids have molecules that are free to move around and flow. This means soli ds do not easily change shape while l iquids will take the shape of their container. As they change back and forth, molecules are gained or lost. The molecules just get locked into place. agine a bucket of Lego bricks. If none of the bricks are put together, they wil l just pour out of the bucket. This would be l ike the molecules in a liquid. Now imagine that someone put all of the little bricks together into one gigantic block and sat that block in the bucket. When you tip the buck et over, the little bricks do not pour out. The big bl ock comes tumbling out as a chun This would be like the molecules in a solid. Liquid water pours but solid ice tumbles. All of the bricks are still there , they just move in a different way. Conservation of Mass tells us that regardless of its phase, the mass of a sample of mat ter is going to stay constant. In the Lego example, there is a constant number of bricks. If you take them apart or put them together , it is still the same number. Mass works the same way. By changing phase, we do not hange the number of molecules. We should not change the mass, either. You will test this idea during the experiment. mainstream_body: PSI Kindergarten: Force and Motion-Colliding balls 5467350 Teacher’s Edition Objective This activity involves rolling and colliding balls to demonstrate the following NGSS standards: PS2.A: Forces and Motion Pushes and pulls can have different strengths and directions. Pushing or pulling on an object can change the speed or direction of its motion and can start or stop it. PS2.B: Types of Interactions When objects touch or collide, they push on one another and can change motion. PS3.C: Relationship Between Energy and Forces A bigger push or pull makes things speed up or slow down more quickly. (secondary) Materials balls of different weight (for example a tennis ball and a basketball) there should be a sufficient number of balls that each pair of students has two to collide Timing 5 minutes organize and explain 5-10 minutes each activity to play and discuss 20-30 minutes total Activity [Answer the questions following each activity] Seat students across from each other on the floor. Have them roll  and catch one ball (heavy or light) at a time. Ask them to notice which one is harder to roll and  which is harder to stop. At the end of this step, ask which takes more force: rolling the heavy ball or the light one (at the same speed)? rolling a faster ball or a slower ball (same weight ball)? stopping the heavy ball or the light one (at the same speed)? stopping a faster ball or a slower ball (same weight ball)? Have the pairs of students swap one ball so that each pair either has 2 heavy or two light balls. Ask the students to roll the balls into each other and watch what happens. Then ask: what makes the balls bounce off each other? (force) what does the force do to the motion of the balls? (change direction and speed) If you like repeat this, where the pairs swap both balls. Have the pairs swap one ball again so that each pair has one of each weight. Repeat rolling the balls into each other. Now ask what was different when the balls collided. (the heavier ball changes motion less than the lighter ball does) PSI Kindergarten: Golf Course 5029200 Teacher’s Edition Description Students conducting this lab will create their own golf course.  Three books, a tennis ball, and a mug will be provided for groups of 3.  The ball must touch all three books and end up in the mug.  Students will learn that the books provide the force that determines the direction of the force on the ball. Materials (per group) 3 heavy books Mug or cup Tennis ball Timing 20-25 minute lab 5 minutes post-lab discussion questions 30 minutes total Post-Lab Discussion Questions When a ball hits a book, why does it change direction? The force of the book on the ball changes the direction. What would happen if we change the direction of a book? Will the ball still end up in the mug? The ball will not go in the mug due to a change in the direction of the force. The first experiment will be a fixed distance experiment: each student will race until the finish line.  1st, 2nd, and 3rd place will be awarded. mainstream_body: I Need Shade Engineering Lab Kindergarten PSI Materials: Snowman 1 white pipe cleaner per student Black p ipe cleaner (cut into sixths, 2 pieces per student 32 UV Pony Beads per student https://www.amazon.com/Korlon-Changing-Sensitive-Reactive- Bracelets/dp/B07F7SRYGD/ref=sr_1_1_sspa?s=arts-crafts&ie=UTF8&qid=1538415066&sr=1-1-spons&keywords=uv+beads&psc=1) Structure Craft sticks Straws Tape Paper Coffee Filters Clay Any other materials you wish for the structure Directions: Day 1: Recite the snowman rhyme I’m a little snowman short and fat, Here’s my scarf and here’s my hat. When I see the sunshine, Here me shout Give me shade and help me out! Tell students that they are going to make a shaded shelter for the snowman but before they do that they need to make the snowman. Give each student 1 white pipe cleaner and 14 uv beads. Have students line up the two ends and fold the pipe cleaner in half. Have the students thread 14 beads onto their pipe cleaner (keeping the beads in the center of the pipe cleaner). Help students twist the pipe cleaner together right above the beads to form a circle with the beads (this will be the bottom circle of the snowman). Give each students 10 more beads and have them thread 5 onto each side of the pipe cleaner. Help students twist the two sides together to form the next circle. Give each student 8 more beads and have them thread 4 onto each side. Help the students twist the two sides together to form the last circle. Give students 2 pieces of the black pipe cleaner. Have them twist one piece around the top of the snowman’s head to form the brim of the hat. Twist the ends of the second piece onto the brim and form a square to make the rest of the hat. Day 2: Lay out all of the supplies on a table Ask student who remembers the snowman’s problem (the sun came out and he could melt) Ask them how we are going to help (make shade for him) Split students into groups of three.
